cse-2001-b-51-a.approach: Prove set equality by a chain of equivalences on an arbitrary set $X$: membership in a powerset is just the subset relation, and "subset of an intersection" splits into two subset conditions.

steps.title: Unfold the definitions
steps.body: For any set $X$: $X \in \mathcal{P}(S) \iff X \subseteq S$. So we must show $X \subseteq A \cap B \iff (X \subseteq A \text{ and } X \subseteq B)$.

steps.title: Chain of equivalences
steps.body:
$$X \in \mathcal{P}(A\cap B) \iff X \subseteq A \cap B \iff \forall x\,(x \in X \Rightarrow x \in A \wedge x \in B)$$
$$\iff (\forall x\,(x\in X \Rightarrow x\in A)) \wedge (\forall x\,(x\in X \Rightarrow x \in B)) \iff X \subseteq A \wedge X \subseteq B$$
$$\iff X \in \mathcal{P}(A) \wedge X \in \mathcal{P}(B) \iff X \in \mathcal{P}(A) \cap \mathcal{P}(B).$$

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: Since every set $X$ belongs to the left side exactly when it belongs to the right side, $\mathcal{P}(A\cap B) = \mathcal{P}(A) \cap \mathcal{P}(B)$. $\blacksquare$

answer.value: $X \in \mathcal{P}(A\cap B) \iff X \subseteq A\cap B \iff X\subseteq A \wedge X \subseteq B \iff X \in \mathcal{P}(A)\cap\mathcal{P}(B)$, so the two sets are equal.

pitfalls: The analogous statement for union is false: $\mathcal{P}(A\cup B) \supseteq \mathcal{P}(A)\cup\mathcal{P}(B)$ only (e.g. $A=\{1\}, B=\{2\}$: $\{1,2\}$ is in the left side only).

cse-2001-b-51-b.approach: Fix $m$ and induct on $n$. The only fact needed is the recursive definition $\text{sum}(k+1) = \text{sum}(k) + (k+1)$.

steps.title: Statement and base case
steps.body:
Let $P(n)$: $\text{sum}(m+n) = \text{sum}(m) + \text{sum}(n) + mn$ for a fixed arbitrary $m$.

Base $n = 0$: LHS $= \text{sum}(m)$; RHS $= \text{sum}(m) + \text{sum}(0) + m\cdot 0 = \text{sum}(m) + 0 + 0$. Equal.

steps.title: Inductive step
steps.body:
Assume $P(n)$. Then
$$\text{sum}(m+n+1) = \text{sum}(m+n) + (m+n+1)$$
$$= \text{sum}(m) + \text{sum}(n) + mn + m + n + 1 \quad (\text{by } P(n))$$
$$= \text{sum}(m) + [\text{sum}(n) + (n+1)] + m(n+1) = \text{sum}(m) + \text{sum}(n+1) + m(n+1).$$
This is exactly $P(n+1)$.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: By induction $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$; since $m$ was arbitrary, the identity holds for all natural $m, n$. $\blacksquare$

answer.value: Induct on $n$: base $n=0$ gives $\text{sum}(m)=\text{sum}(m)+0+0$; step: $\text{sum}(m+n+1)=\text{sum}(m)+\text{sum}(n)+mn+(m+n+1)=\text{sum}(m)+\text{sum}(n+1)+m(n+1)$.

pitfalls: Regroup $mn + m + n + 1$ as $(n+1) + m(n+1)$ — the $(n+1)$ completes $\text{sum}(n+1)$, the rest is $m(n+1)$.

cse-2001-b-52-a.approach: Use unique factorisation of a positive integer into (power of 2) × (odd number): equal outputs force equal powers of 2 and then equal odd parts.
concepts: Highest power of 2 dividing an integer

steps.title: Assume equal images
steps.body: Suppose $h(a,b) = h(c,d)$. Adding 1: $(2a+1)2^b = (2c+1)2^d$.

steps.title: Compare powers of 2
steps.body: $2a+1$ and $2c+1$ are odd, so the exact power of 2 dividing the left side is $2^b$ and the right side $2^d$. Equal numbers have the same exact power of 2, so $b = d$.

steps.title: Compare odd parts
steps.body: Dividing by $2^b = 2^d$: $2a+1 = 2c+1 \Rightarrow a = c$. Hence $(a,b) = (c,d)$ and $h$ is one-one. $\blacksquare$

answer.value: $(2a+1)2^b=(2c+1)2^d$ ⇒ $b=d$ (exact power of 2 dividing the number) ⇒ $2a+1=2c+1$ ⇒ $a=c$; so $h$ is injective.

pitfalls: Do not divide without justifying $b=d$ first; the argument rests on the odd factor having no factor 2.

cse-2001-b-52-b.approach: Given any $n$, factor $n+1 \ge 1$ as $2^b \times$ odd; the odd part is $2a+1$ for a unique $a \ge 0$, which gives the preimage.
concepts: Factorisation into power of 2 and odd part

steps.title: Target equation
steps.body: For $n \in N$ we need $a,b \in N$ with $(2a+1)2^b - 1 = n$, i.e. $(2a+1)2^b = n+1$.

steps.title: Construct the preimage
steps.body: Since $n + 1 \ge 1$, let $b$ be the largest integer with $2^b \mid n+1$ (exists, $b \ge 0$). Then $k = (n+1)/2^b$ is odd and $k \ge 1$, so $k = 2a+1$ with $a = (k-1)/2 \in N$.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: $h(a,b) = (2a+1)2^b - 1 = k\cdot 2^b - 1 = (n+1) - 1 = n$. Every $n$ has a preimage, so $h$ is onto; with part (a), $h$ is a bijection $N\times N \to N$. $\blacksquare$

answer.value: For any $n$, write $n+1 = 2^b(2a+1)$ (strip all factors of 2); then $h(a,b) = n$, so $h$ is onto.

pitfalls: The "$-1$" in $h$ is what makes $0$ reachable: $h(0,0)=0$. Without it, $0$ would have no preimage.

cse-2001-b-53-a.approach: Pattern-matching (KMP-style) DFA: state $q_i$ = length of the longest prefix of $baab$ that is a suffix of the input read so far; $q_4$ is a trap-accept state.

steps.title: States
steps.body: $q_0$: no progress, $q_1$: seen $b$, $q_2$: seen $ba$, $q_3$: seen $baa$, $q_4$: seen $baab$ (accepting, stays there).

steps.title: Mismatch transitions
steps.body:
For each wrong symbol take the longest prefix of $baab$ that is a suffix of the new string:

| state | read | string | goes to |
|---|---|---|---|
| $q_0$ | a | a | $q_0$ |
| $q_1$ | b | bb | $q_1$ ("b") |
| $q_2$ | b | bab | $q_1$ ("b") |
| $q_3$ | a | baaa | $q_0$ |
| $q_4$ | a,b | — | $q_4$ |

steps.title: Trace a string
steps.body: Input $abbaab$: $q_0 \xrightarrow{a} q_0 \xrightarrow{b} q_1 \xrightarrow{b} q_1 \xrightarrow{a} q_2 \xrightarrow{a} q_3 \xrightarrow{b} q_4$ — accepted. Input $babaa$ ends in $q_3$ — rejected.

pitfalls: From $q_2$ ("ba") on b the string ends in "b", so go to $q_1$, not $q_0$.
From $q_3$ ("baa") on a no suffix of "baaa" is a prefix of baab, so go to $q_0$.
cse-2001-b-53-a.verification: Minimal: states $q_0..q_3$ are distinguished by the shortest completing suffix ($baab, aab, ab, b$), and $q_4$ is the only accepting state — 5 states are necessary.

cse-2001-b-53-b.approach: Track two independent parities. Product of two 2-state parity DFAs gives 4 states; accept only when both counts are odd.

steps.title: States
steps.body: State = (parity of #a, parity of #b): $EE, EO, OE, OO$. Start $EE$ (empty string has 0 a's and 0 b's), accept $OO$.

steps.title: Transitions
steps.body:
Reading $a$ flips the first letter, reading $b$ flips the second:

| state | a | b |
|---|---|---|
| $\to EE$ | $OE$ | $EO$ |
| $EO$ | $OO$ | $EE$ |
| $OE$ | $EE$ | $OO$ |
| $*OO$ | $EO$ | $OE$ |

steps.title: Check
steps.body: $ab$: $EE \xrightarrow{a} OE \xrightarrow{b} OO$ — accepted (1 a, 1 b). $aab$: $EE\to OE\to EE\to EO$ — rejected (2 a's).

answer.value: 4 states (a-parity, b-parity) $=EE,EO,OE,OO$; a toggles the first, b the second; start $EE$, accept $OO$.

pitfalls: A 3-state answer is impossible: all four parity combinations are pairwise distinguishable.
cse-2001-b-53-b.verification: Each pair of states is distinguished by one of $\varepsilon, a, b, ab$, so the 4-state DFA is minimal.

cse-2001-b-54.approach: Push two symbols per $a$, switch state on $c$, pop one symbol per $b$; when the bottom marker reappears, move to the final state by an $\varepsilon$-move. Every move is forced, so the PDA is deterministic.

steps.title: Idea
steps.body: Each $a$ must be matched by two $b$'s, so push $XX$ for every $a$; after $c$ pop one $X$ per $b$. $n \ge 1$ means $c$ must be read with an $X$ (not $Z_0$) on top.

steps.title: Transition function
steps.body:
$P = (\{q_0,q_1,q_f\}, \{a,b,c\}, \{X, Z_0\}, \delta, q_0, Z_0, \{q_f\})$:

| move | result |
|---|---|
| $\delta(q_0, a, Z_0)$ | $(q_0, XXZ_0)$ |
| $\delta(q_0, a, X)$ | $(q_0, XXX)$ |
| $\delta(q_0, c, X)$ | $(q_1, X)$ |
| $\delta(q_1, b, X)$ | $(q_1, \varepsilon)$ |
| $\delta(q_1, \varepsilon, Z_0)$ | $(q_f, Z_0)$ |

All other moves undefined (reject). Acceptance state: $q_f$ (acceptance by final state).

steps.title: Determinism
steps.body: For every (state, top) pair at most one move applies; the only $\varepsilon$-move is on $(q_1, Z_0)$, and $q_1$ has no input move on $Z_0$. So it is a DPDA.

steps.title: Trace acbb
steps.body: $(q_0, acbb, Z_0) \vdash (q_0, cbb, XXZ_0) \vdash (q_1, bb, XXZ_0) \vdash (q_1, b, XZ_0) \vdash (q_1, \varepsilon, Z_0) \vdash (q_f, \varepsilon, Z_0)$ — accepted. $acb$ stops in $q_1$ with $X$ on top — rejected; $cbb$ has no move on $(q_0,c,Z_0)$ — rejected.

answer.value: $\delta(q_0,a,Z_0)=(q_0,XXZ_0)$; $\delta(q_0,a,X)=(q_0,XXX)$; $\delta(q_0,c,X)=(q_1,X)$; $\delta(q_1,b,X)=(q_1,\varepsilon)$; $\delta(q_1,\varepsilon,Z_0)=(q_f,Z_0)$; accept by final state $q_f$.

pitfalls: Defining $\delta(q_0,c,Z_0)$ would wrongly accept $c$ ($n=0$).
Extra $b$'s: in $q_f$ there are no moves, so $acbbb$ is rejected.
cse-2001-b-54.verification: Traced $aacbbbb$: after $aa$ the stack is $XXXXZ_0$, four $b$'s pop it to $Z_0$, then $\varepsilon$ to $q_f$ — accepted; $aacbbb$ ends with $X$ on top — rejected.

cse-2001-b-55-a.approach: X is (on valid inputs) exactly the complement of the halting problem HALT. Decidable languages are closed under complement, so a decider for X would yield a decider for HALT.

steps.title: Relate X to HALT
steps.body: HALT $= \{\langle M, w\rangle : M \text{ halts on } w\}$. $M$ loops forever on $w$ iff $M$ does not halt on $w$, so $X = \overline{\text{HALT}}$ (over well-formed encodings).

steps.title: Reduction
steps.body: Suppose a TM $D$ decides $X$. Build $D'$: on $\langle M,w\rangle$ run $D$ and output the opposite answer. $D'$ always halts and accepts exactly HALT — so HALT would be decidable.

steps.title: Contradiction
steps.body: HALT is undecidable (given), so no such $D$ exists: X is undecidable. $\blacksquare$

answer.value: $X$ is the complement of HALT; a decider for $X$ with its answer flipped would decide HALT, contradiction — so $X$ is undecidable.

pitfalls: Malformed encodings are a fixed decidable set and do not affect the argument.
cse-2001-b-55-a.verification: Consistent with part (b): X is co-RE (its complement HALT is RE) but neither recursive nor RE.

cse-2001-b-55-b.approach: Use the theorem: if a language and its complement are both partially decidable (RE), it is decidable. HALT is RE but undecidable, so its complement X cannot be RE.

steps.title: Theorem
steps.body: If $L$ and $\overline{L}$ are both RE, run their recognisers in parallel (alternating steps) on input $x$; exactly one accepts, so the combined machine always halts and decides $L$.

steps.title: Apply to X
steps.body: HALT is partially decidable (given: simulate $M$ on $w$, accept if it halts). If $X = \overline{\text{HALT}}$ were also partially decidable, the theorem would make HALT decidable.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: HALT is undecidable, so X is not partially decidable (not RE). $\blacksquare$

answer.value: If $X$ were partially decidable, HALT and its complement $X$ would both be RE, making HALT decidable — contradiction; so $X$ is not even partially decidable.

pitfalls: Just running $M$ on $w$ cannot confirm looping: the simulation never gives a "yes, it loops" answer in finite time.
cse-2001-b-55-b.verification: Standard classification: HALT is RE but not recursive, so its complement is co-RE, not recursive and not RE.

cse-2001-b-56-a.approach: Capacity is simply the product of surfaces, tracks, sectors and sector size.
cse-2001-b-56-a.given:
| item | value |
|---|---|
| surfaces | 20 |
| tracks/surface | 1000 |
| sectors/track | 16 |
| sector size | 1 KB |
| speed | 3000 rpm |

steps.title: Multiply
steps.body: $$20 \times 1000 \times 16 \times 1\text{ KB} = 320\,000\text{ KB}$$

answer.value: $20 \times 1000 \times 16 \times 1\text{ KB} = 320\,000$ KB $= 312.5$ MB

pitfalls: Tracks/surface is per surface: multiply by all 20 surfaces.

cse-2001-b-56-b.approach: One full track passes under the head per revolution, so transfer rate = (bytes per track) × (revolutions per second).
cse-2001-b-56-b.given:
| item | value |
|---|---|
| surfaces | 20 |
| tracks/surface | 1000 |
| sectors/track | 16 |
| sector size | 1 KB |
| speed | 3000 rpm |

steps.title: Revolutions per second
steps.body: $3000\text{ rpm} = 3000/60 = 50$ rev/s (one revolution = 20 ms).

steps.title: Rate
steps.body: Track capacity $= 16 \times 1\text{ KB} = 16$ KB. Rate $= 16\text{ KB} \times 50 = 800$ KB/s $= 800 \times 1024 = 819\,200$ bytes/s.

answer.value: $16\text{ KB/rev} \times 50\text{ rev/s} = 800$ KB/s ($819\,200$ B/s)

pitfalls: Number of surfaces does not affect the rate: only one head transfers at a time.
cse-2001-b-56-b.verification: One sector takes $20/16 = 1.25$ ms, i.e. 1 KB per 1.25 ms $= 800$ KB/s.

cse-2001-b-56-c.approach: A byte arrives every $1/(\text{rate})$ seconds; for each byte the CPU spends interrupt overhead + one memory write. CPU share = (CPU time per byte) / (byte arrival time).
cse-2001-b-56-c.given:
| item | value |
|---|---|
| transfer rate | 800 KB/s |
| memory read/write | 0.1 µs/byte |
| interrupt overhead | 0.4 µs |

steps.title: CPU time per byte
steps.body: Each byte raises an interrupt: $0.4\ \mu s$ overhead $+ 0.1\ \mu s$ to move the byte to memory $= 0.5\ \mu s$.

steps.title: Percentage
steps.body:
$$\frac{0.5}{1.2207} \times 100 \approx 40.96\% \approx 41\%$$
(With 1 KB = 1000 B, $t_{byte}=1.25\ \mu s$ and the share is $40\%$.)

answer.value: $\approx 41\%$ ($0.5\ \mu s$ CPU per byte out of $\approx 1.22\ \mu s$ per byte)

pitfalls: Include the 0.1 µs memory transfer as well as the 0.4 µs interrupt overhead — in interrupt-driven I/O the CPU does the transfer itself.
cse-2001-b-56-c.verification: Per sector: 1024 bytes × 0.5 µs = 512 µs of CPU in a 1.25 ms sector time → $512/1250 = 40.96\%$.

cse-2001-b-56-d.approach: In cycle-stealing DMA the CPU is blocked only for the memory cycle stolen per byte; set-up overhead is negligible. Share = stolen time per byte / byte time.

steps.title: Stolen time per byte
steps.body: The DMA controller steals one memory cycle per byte: $0.1\ \mu s$. Initialisation/termination overhead is negligible (given).

steps.title: Percentage
steps.body:
Byte time $= 1.2207\ \mu s$ (part c):
$$\frac{0.1}{1.2207}\times 100 \approx 8.19\% \approx 8.2\%$$

answer.value: $\approx 8.2\%$ ($0.1\ \mu s$ stolen per $\approx 1.22\ \mu s$ byte time)

pitfalls: The interrupt overhead does not apply per byte under DMA — at most one interrupt per sector, which is negligible.
cse-2001-b-56-d.verification: Per sector: $1024 \times 0.1 = 102.4\ \mu s$ out of $1250\ \mu s$ → $8.19\%$; it is the maximum because DMA requests are always granted.

cse-2001-b-57-a.given:
| item | value |
|---|---|
| address | 32 bits |
| cache | 256 KB $=2^{18}$ B |
| block | 16 B $=2^4$ |
| associativity | 4-way |
pitfalls: Dividing by the block size only gives the number of lines (16384), not sets.

cse-2001-b-57-b.approach: Tag = address bits − set-index bits − offset bits.
cse-2001-b-57-b.given:
| item | value |
|---|---|
| address | 32 bits |
| cache | 256 KB $=2^{18}$ B |
| block | 16 B $=2^4$ |
| associativity | 4-way |

steps.title: Index and offset
steps.body: Offset $= \log_2 16 = 4$ bits; set index $= \log_2 4096 = 12$ bits.

steps.title: Tag
steps.body: $32 - 12 - 4 = 16$ bits. Address split (tag, set, offset) $= 16 + 12 + 4$ bits.

answer.value: 16 bits

pitfalls: Using the line count ($2^{14}$, 14 bits) as the index gives the direct-mapped tag (14 bits) instead.

cse-2001-b-57-c.approach: All ways of the selected set are searched in parallel: one comparator per way, each as wide as the tag.
cse-2001-b-57-c.given:
| item | value |
|---|---|
| address | 32 bits |
| cache | 256 KB $=2^{18}$ B |
| block | 16 B $=2^4$ |
| associativity | 4-way |

steps.title: Number
steps.body: The set index selects one set of 4 lines; their tags are compared simultaneously → 4 comparators.

steps.title: Width
steps.body: Each compares the 16-bit tag (part b) → 16-bit comparators.

answer.value: 4 comparators, each 16 bits wide

pitfalls: Not 4096 × 4: comparators are shared across sets, only the selected set is compared.
cse-2001-b-57-c.verification: k-way associative ⇒ k comparators of tag width; here $k=4$, tag $=16$.

steps.title: Compute
steps.body: Block $= 16 = 2^4$ bytes, so $\log_2 16 = 4$ bits select a byte within the block.

steps.title: Place in the address
steps.body: Address split (tag, set, offset) $= 16 + 12 + 4$ bits.

answer.value: 4 bits

pitfalls: Associativity does not change the offset width.
cse-2001-b-57-d.verification: 4 bits address offsets 0–15, exactly the 16 bytes of a block.

cse-2001-b-57-e.approach: Tag storage = (number of lines) × (tag bits per line).
cse-2001-b-57-e.given:
| item | value |
|---|---|
| address | 32 bits |
| cache | 256 KB $=2^{18}$ B |
| block | 16 B $=2^4$ |
| associativity | 4-way |
pitfalls: Valid/dirty bits are not asked — only tag bits.
cse-2001-b-57-e.verification: Equivalently 4096 sets × 4 ways × 2 bytes per tag $= 32768$ bytes.

cse-2001-b-58-a.approach: A 3-variable function is self-dual iff $f(\bar x) = \overline{f(x)}$, i.e. of every complementary minterm pair $(m, 7-m)$ exactly one is a minterm.

steps.title: Verdict
steps.body:
Every pair contributes exactly one minterm, so $f(\bar a, \bar b, \bar c) = \overline{f(a,b,c)}$ for all inputs, i.e. $f^d = f$. **Yes, $f$ is self-dual.**

Indeed $f = 1$ iff at most one variable is 1, i.e. $f = \bar a\bar b + \bar b \bar c + \bar a \bar c = \text{MAJ}(\bar a, \bar b, \bar c)$, and majority is self-dual.

answer.value: Yes — of each complementary pair $(0,7),(1,6),(2,5),(3,4)$ exactly one is a minterm, so $f^d(a,b,c) = \overline{f(\bar a,\bar b,\bar c)} = f$.

pitfalls: A self-dual function of $n$ variables must have exactly $2^{n-1}$ minterms (here 4); having 4 is necessary but the pair test is what proves it.
cse-2001-b-58-a.verification: Dual of $\bar a\bar b + \bar b\bar c + \bar a\bar c$ is $(\bar a+\bar b)(\bar b+\bar c)(\bar a+\bar c)$, which expands back to $\bar a\bar b + \bar b\bar c + \bar a\bar c$.

cse-2001-b-58-b.approach: Tabulate the 10 valid excess-3 codes (3–12) with the codes 0, 1, 2, 13, 14, 15 as don't-cares, then group the 0s of the $b_4$ column on a K-map.

steps.title: Minimal POS
steps.body:
$$b_4 = (\bar e_4 + e_2)(\bar e_4 + e_1)(e_4 + \bar e_2 + \bar e_1)$$
Three sum terms are necessary (3 cannot share a term with 4/5/6/12). Equivalently $b_4 = \overline{e_4 \oplus e_2e_1}$.

steps.title: If b4 means the MSB
steps.body: The scan's subscripts are blurred. If the outputs were labelled $b_4b_3b_2b_1$ with $b_4$ the MSB (digit 8, 9 ⇒ E = 11, 12), the same method gives $b_{4} = e_{4}(e_3 + e_2)(e_3 + e_1)$ with inputs $e_4e_3e_2e_1$ (zeros 3–10, don't-cares as above).

answer.value: $b_4 = (\bar e_4 + e_2)(\bar e_4 + e_1)(e_4 + \bar e_2 + \bar e_1)$ (weight-4 output; labels read as 8-4-2-1). If $b_4$ is instead the MSB (labels $e_4..e_1$): $b_4 = e_4(e_3+e_2)(e_3+e_1)$.

pitfalls: Forgetting the six unused codes as don't-cares gives a much larger expression.
BCD bit $b_4$ is 1 for digits 4–7, i.e. excess-3 inputs 7–10.

cse-2001-b-59-a.approach: Mealy machine with two modes (copy / complement), each split by whether the last input already starts the switching pair. The bit that completes "00" is still copied; the bit that completes "11" is still complemented.

steps.title: States
steps.body:
| state | mode | remembers |
|---|---|---|
| A | copy | last input not 0 (or start) |
| B | copy | last input 0 |
| C | complement | last input not 1 |
| D | complement | last input 1 |

steps.title: Transitions (input/output)
steps.body:
- A: 1/1 → A, 0/0 → B
- B: 1/1 → A, 0/0 → C (second 0: copied, then switch)
- C: 0/1 → C, 1/0 → D
- D: 0/1 → C, 1/0 → A (second 1: complemented, then switch back)

steps.title: Check against the example
steps.body: Input 101100: A→A→B→A→A→B→C, output 101100. Input 01001011 from C: C→C→D→C→C→D→C→D→A, output 10110100. Input 011 from A: output 011. All match the given streams.

answer.value: 4-state Mealy machine: A (copy), B (copy, last 0), C (complement), D (complement, last 1). A: 0/0→B, 1/1→A; B: 0/0→C, 1/1→A; C: 0/1→C, 1/0→D; D: 0/1→C, 1/0→A.

pitfalls: The second 0 is output as 0 (copied); complementing starts with the next bit — check this against the example stream.
cse-2001-b-59-a.verification: Replayed the full 17-bit example stream through the diagram; every output bit matches.

cse-2001-b-59-b.approach: Encode A=00, B=01, C=10, D=11 ($Q_1$ = mode, $Q_0$ = "last bit could start the switch"), build the next-state table, then read J/K from the JK excitation table.

steps.title: Flip-flop Q0 and output
steps.body:
$Q_0=0$ rows (00, 10): $Q_0^+=1$ at $(Q_1,x)=(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ ⇒ $J_0 = \bar Q_1 \bar x + Q_1 x$.

$Q_0=1$ rows (01, 11): $Q_0^+ = 0$ always ⇒ $K_0 = 1$.

Output: $z = x$ in copy mode, $\bar x$ in complement mode ⇒ $z = x \oplus Q_1$.

answer.value: With A=00, B=01, C=10, D=11 ($Q_1$ = mode): $J_1 = Q_0\bar x$, $K_1 = Q_0 x$; $J_0 = Q_1 x + \bar Q_1 \bar x$, $K_0 = 1$; output $z = x \oplus Q_1$.

pitfalls: The expressions depend on the state assignment; any consistent assignment is acceptable, but the J/K must match its own table.
"S-K" in the question is the J-K master-slave flip-flop.
cse-2001-b-59-b.verification: Checked $Q^+ = J\bar Q + \bar K Q$ on all 8 rows, e.g. state 11, $x=1$: $Q_1^+ = 0\cdot 0 + \overline{1}\cdot 1 = 0$, $Q_0^+ = J_0\cdot 0 + \bar 1 \cdot 1 = 0$ → 00 ✓.

cse-2001-b-60-a.approach: List each instruction's destination and sources, then check every earlier→later pair for RAW (write then read), WAR (read then write) and WAW (write then write) on the same register.
cse-2001-b-60-a.given:
| instr | writes | reads |
|---|---|---|
| I1 | r2 | r3, r4 |
| I2 | r4 | r2, r3 |
| I3 | memory | r2, r1 |
| I4 | r3 | r4, r2 |

steps.title: RAW (true) dependencies
steps.body:
- I1 → I2 on r2
- I1 → I3 on r2
- I1 → I4 on r2
- I2 → I4 on r4

steps.title: WAR (anti) dependencies
steps.body:
- I1 → I2 on r4 (I1 reads r4, I2 writes it)
- I1 → I4 on r3 (I1 reads r3, I4 writes it)
- I2 → I4 on r3 (I2 reads r3, I4 writes it)

steps.title: WAW (output)
steps.body: Destinations r2, r4, memory, r3 are all different — no WAW. I3 writes only memory and nothing later touches memory.

pitfalls: sw has no destination register; r2 is a source (the value stored) together with r1.
cse-2001-b-60-a.verification: Checked all 6 ordered pairs (I1,I2), (I1,I3), (I1,I4), (I2,I3), (I2,I4), (I3,I4); (I2,I3) and (I3,I4) share no written register.

cse-2001-b-60-b.approach: Only RAW dependencies can become hazards in an in-order 5-stage pipeline. With write in the first half and read in the second half of a cycle, a RAW is a hazard only if the consumer's ID comes before the producer's WB cycle.

steps.title: Timing without stalls
steps.body: I1 WB in cycle 5, I2 WB in cycle 6. Register reads happen in ID: I2 in cycle 3, I3 in cycle 4, I4 in cycle 5.

steps.title: Check each RAW
steps.body:
| RAW | producer WB | consumer ID | hazard? |
|---|---|---|---|
| I1→I2 (r2) | 5 | 3 | yes |
| I1→I3 (r2) | 5 | 4 | yes |
| I1→I4 (r2) | 5 | 5 | no (write 1st half, read 2nd half) |
| I2→I4 (r4) | 6 | 5 | yes |

steps.title: WAR / WAW
steps.body: In this in-order pipeline every read (ID) precedes later instructions' writes (WB), and writes complete in program order, so WAR and WAW never become hazards.

answer.value: RAW hazards I1→I2 (r2), I1→I3 (r2) and I2→I4 (r4); I1→I4 is not a hazard (split-cycle register file); WAR/WAW cannot occur in this in-order pipeline.

pitfalls: I1→I4 is resolved by the write-first-half / read-second-half register file — do not count it.
cse-2001-b-60-b.verification: A RAW is safe without forwarding only when the producer is at least 3 instructions ahead; the three hazards have distances 1, 2 and 2, while I1→I4 has distance 3.

cse-2001-b-60-c.approach: Every producer is an ALU instruction (sub), so its result exists at the end of EX; forwarding from the EX/MEM and MEM/WB latches reaches each consumer in time. Only a load-use RAW would need a stall, and there is none.

steps.title: Forwarding paths
steps.body:
- I1→I2 (r2): I1 result ready end of cycle 3, I2 EX in cycle 4 → EX/MEM → EX forward.
- I1→I3 (r2): I3 EX in cycle 5 (and it needs the store data only in MEM, cycle 6) → MEM/WB → EX forward.
- I2→I4 (r4): I2 result end of cycle 4, I4 EX in cycle 6 → MEM/WB → EX forward.

scene.caption: All three hazards forwarded, no stalls

steps.title: Verdict
steps.body: No instruction is a load, so no value is produced later than the end of EX; all hazards are removed by forwarding with zero stalls. **Yes.**

answer.value: Yes — all producers are ALU (sub) instructions, so their results can be forwarded to the dependent instructions' EX stage; no load-use hazard exists, hence no stalls.

pitfalls: Forwarding fails only for a load followed immediately by a use; sw is a store, not a load.
cse-2001-b-60-c.verification: Total time with forwarding = $5 + 3 = 8$ cycles, the ideal for 4 instructions in a 5-stage pipeline.
